per_quote.text: The goal of the present research was to examine how political climate moderates the relationship between self-reported political conservatism and COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake.
Controlling for age, education, income, and race, there was an interaction between political conservatism and conservative political climate for both vaccine and booster hesitancy
However, conservatives living in liberal political climates were less vaccine hesitant than their conservative counterparts living in conservative regions.
We collected online survey data from 683 participants between March 8 and April 19, 2023.
This was an online self-reported study in which a nonprobability convenience sample was recruited from the United States between March 8 and April 19, 2023.
We assessed regional political climate using zip code data provided by participants and 2020 presidential election results sourced from the New York Times.
when controlling for age, education, income, race, and vaccine access, political conservatism and conservative regional climate were positively associated with vaccine hesitancy
Additionally, the interaction between political conservatism and conservative regional climate was significant
The interaction for vaccine hesitancy indicates that at the lowest levels of conservatism i.e., liberalism vaccine hesitancy is lower regardless of regional climate.
The most conservative participants in liberal climates were 60% likely to get boosted, while conservatives in conservative climates were less than 35% likely to get boosted
there was no significant differences based on gender or race for vaccine hesitancy, booster hesitancy, vaccine status, or booster status.

Another limitation in this dataset is the reliance on self-reported vaccine status. Self-report is susceptible to social desirability and recall bias, and we cannot assume that reported vaccine status reflects actual vaccine status.
Further, our sample includes only White and Black participants recruited through Qualtrics Panels, and may not generalize to broader populations in the United States.
There is an emerging body of evidence that the broader political climate within which an individual lives can influence COVID-19 vaccine hesitancy and uptake.

Analyzing over 50 million tweets from late 2020—a critical period of polarizing discourse during the pandemic’s early phase—we examine regional variations in discussions surrounding three key health interventions: lockdowns, masks, and vaccines.

We collected a large-scale dataset of COVID-19 political discussions on Twitter (now X) occurring between October 9, 2020, to January 4, 2021, comprising approximately 12.5 million tweets linked to the United States and 46.6 million tweets linked to Canada.

We demonstrate a strong negative correlation between regional vaccination rates and the degree of polarization in vaccine-related discussions in the U.S., suggesting tangible public health implications of online partisan division.
By tracking the temporal evolution of polarization, we identify distinct spikes linked to specific political events and policy announcements.
These polarization surges typically lasted only a few days, revealing the dynamic nature of online partisan discourse.

The geographic heterogeneity in polarization patterns—with certain conservative states showing unexpectedly low polarization and some liberal states displaying high polarization—highlights the complex interplay between political ideology, policy implementation, and public response during health crises.
This relationship was notably weaker in Canada, pointing to important cross-national differences in how political polarization manifests and impacts health behaviors.
Our findings reveal that conservative regions in both countries exhibited higher overall polarization levels regarding these topics.

While our polarization index reflects the discourse of politically engaged Twitter users, it nevertheless captures key dynamics of online debate that influence public narratives and align with observable regional outcomes.

While our study focuses on the COVID-19 context, the proposed methodology for quantifying partisan polarization at scale can be adapted to examine large-scale discussions across various temporal, spatial, and topical dimensions.
Recent computational approaches increasingly draw on text embedding methods to study polarization, using contextualized representations to detect partisan divides across topics and communities.
Consequently, our study adopts a strictly text-based method, which remains both accessible and scalable for analyzing large-scale digital discourse.

Extensive research now confirms that in the U.S., Democratic Party supporters were consistently more likely to adhere to social distancing guidelines [8–10], wear masks [11,12], and get vaccinated [13–15] compared to their Republican counterparts.

A growing body of research confirms that online pandemic discussions [9,25–27] exhibited distinct regional patterns characterized by the same partisan animosity that influenced heterogeneous implementation of public health measures [25] and subsequent epidemiological outcomes [9].

Results suggest that exposure to the Trump advertisement with the “convicted criminal” label had significant, negative impacts on Democrats’ perceptions of individuals with records, but improved perceived feelings of representation.

Online political hostility is positively associated with these indicators, with the strongest associations for political interest, political knowledge, and online participation.
The greater engagement of hostile social media users may thus provide them with a higher reacher than other users.
We rely on a data infrastructure combining panel survey data with online behavioral data from X (see also [59]).
The total number of panelists where we were able to link survey responses to their X handle in this period was 2567.
During this period, we managed to scrape 9,250,180 posts from our panelists.

Fig 1 demonstrate positive and statistically significant associations between online political hostility and several indicators of political engagement and its antecedents (consistent with Expectation 1).

The associations with online participation and political interest are, for example, 0.236 (95% CI [0.186; 0.285]) and 0.306 (95% CI [0.247; 0.366]) for online political hostility, whereas they are 0.176 (95% CI [0.103; 0.249]) and 0.170 (95% CI [0.086; 0.253]) for AFINN scores

The descriptive pattern suggests that the association between engagement and hostility is often stronger among more affectively polarized users: for those low on affective polarization only four out of eighteen associations, across our three measures of online hostility, are significant, whereas for those high on affective polarization fourteen out of eighteen are significant.
The count-model results indicate that higher political hostility is associated with more posts and with larger numbers of followers and, to a lesser extent, friends.

A change from the mean level of hostility to 1.5 standard deviations above the mean is associated with an increase in the number of posts from around 420 to around 900 and an increase in the number of followers from around 220 to around 370.

Classical research on political behavior emphasizes that education, internal efficacy, political interest, political knowledge, and participation are central to democratic engagement.

We extend this revisionist perspective to online political hostility by asking whether hostile political expression on X/Twitter is associated not only with deprivation or personality-based explanations, but also with political engagement and its antecedents.
Here, we extend and integrate the study of the negative side of political engagement into the study of online politics with a specific focus on online political hostility.
Within the classical literature, political engagement has been seen as a boon to democracy.
At the same time, even in this classical literature, it was explicitly acknowledged that political engagement could go too far.

American Indian (AI) adolescents experience disproportionately high rates of substance use, yet the role of substance use and other individual characteristics in friendship network formation within AI-majority reservation schools remains understudied.
This study examines the structural and relational foundations of friendship networks among AI adolescents in their unique cultural context.
These findings reveal a distinct relational ecology within AI-majority reservation schools, where peer ties are organized around structural and demographic commonalities rather than risky behaviors.

These findings challenge assumptions underpinning many network-based prevention programs and underscore the critical need for theories and interventions that are culturally and contextually grounded in the lived experiences of AI youth.

Using social network data from 9th and 10th-grade students (N = 247) across three schools on a Northern Plains reservation, we employed exponential random graph models (ERGMs) to analyze factors shaping friendship ties.
This study addresses this gap by collecting and analyzing first-hand social network data from 9th- and 10th-grade students in three schools on a Northern Plains reservation.

We had an overall response rate of 77% across the three schools. Specifically, 72% of eligible students completed surveys in School A (n = 52 out of 72), 76% in School B (n = 140 out of 184), and 84% in School C (n = 71 out of 84), for a total sample size of 263.

Of the 247 participants with complete network data, item non-response was limited to the substance use variables. Specifically, 16 participants (6.5%) selected ‘Refuse to answer’ for alcohol use, 14 (5.7%) for tobacco use, and 21 (8.5%) for marijuana use.
Results indicated that universal structural mechanisms (reciprocity, transitivity) and demographic homophily (gender, grade, sexual orientation) were primary drivers of friendship.
However, unlike what is often observed in studies of other adolescent populations, substance use showed no consistent association with sending ties or receiving ties.
Similarly, depression and AI identity were not substantively associated with friendship formation.
Strong and significant homophily was present for gender and grade across all schools, indicating that shared gender identity and grade level are primary axes of friendship formation.

Most notably, School C was the only setting where incoming ties were significantly centralized (negative GWIDeg), indicating a pronounced popularity hierarchy in which a small subset of students received disproportionately many nominations.

First, we recognize that the results presented here represent only three schools on one reservation. The history, policies, geography, and culture of this reservation all intersect with network formation and maintenance patterns.
Our findings may not extend to AI youth in racially heterogeneous schools, where Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17] observed different network characteristics.

More importantly, cross-sectional ERGMs cannot analytically distinguish selection processes—adolescents choosing friends with similar attributes—from influence processes—friends becoming more similar to one another over time.
Furthermore, we acknowledge that these data reflect only one developmental epoch of adolescents at one time point.

By focusing on reservation schools, where AI youth are the norm rather than a statistical minority, this research moves beyond generalizations derived from prior research and contributes new insights into the unique architecture of AI adolescent social worlds.
This paper takes an initial step toward understanding these dynamics by investigating the role of substance use in the formation of friendship ties within AI-majority schools.

One study that did focus specifically on AI youth network characteristics is Rees, Freng, and Winfree [17], who used Add Health to describe AI networks in heterogeneous school contexts, finding that AI adolescents had fewer reciprocated friendships than White peers.

Research in diverse school settings has consistently demonstrated that substance use is linked to friendship ties, often through processes of selection (youth choosing friends with similar behaviors) and influence (friends shaping one another’s conduct).
